claims.text: A controlled cooling rate followed by secondary annealing will induce nanoscale tungsten carbide precipitates in an HfNbTaTiZr-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
The modified heat treatment will produce a uniform dispersion of tungsten carbide precipitates.
The tungsten carbide precipitates will be located at grain boundaries and intergranular regions.
The precipitate size and distribution can be controlled through the proposed heat-treatment protocol.
Finely dispersed tungsten carbide precipitates will form thermally conductive bridges across the disordered HEA matrix.
These conductive bridges will enhance electron and phonon transport.
The tungsten carbide precipitates will pin grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary pinning will limit grain coarsening during high-temperature cyclic loading and irradiation.
Limiting grain coarsening will preserve the alloy's mechanical strength under the proposed operating conditions.
The optimized treatment will increase thermal conductivity by more than approximately 15–20% relative to an untreated or conventionally heat-treated HEA.
The conductivity improvement will be accompanied by only a minimal reduction in yield strength.
The treated alloy will retain resistance to thermal fatigue under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
The treated alloy will retain resistance to irradiation-induced degradation.
The proposed benefits are expected to hold between 600°C and 800°C under cyclic thermal/mechanical loading and representative irradiation.

contradictions.description: The example initial alloy is HfNbTaTiZr and the sole intervention is heat treatment, yet the proposed mediator is tungsten carbide. No tungsten or carbon source, pre-existing W/C content, or compositional addition is specified, so the intervention cannot coherently account for formation of the stated precipitate.
